key: From pleasure comes grief, from pleasure comes fear; he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear.
s: Here the chapter begins tracing grief and fear to five sources in turn; the Theravāda commentary, story XVI.2, reads it as comfort for a layman weeping daily at the burning-ground for his dead son: sorrow and fear arise only from one held dear.
src: The Theravāda commentary, Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā XVI.2 (on verse 212), trans. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends, vol. 3 (1921), Norman pp. 276 to 278

evidence.words: The story goes that this layman, on losing his son, was so overwhelmed with grief that he went every day to the burning-ground and wept … Therefore grieve not at the thought that your dear son is dead. For whether sorrow or fear arises, it arises solely because of one that is dear.
evidence.gloss: Story XVI.2: a layman who had lost his son went every day to the cremation ground and wept; the Teacher tells him not to grieve for his dead son, for sorrow or fear, whenever it arises, arises only on account of one who is dear, and speaks verse 212. The Pali explanation agrees: sorrow or fear arises only in dependence on a dear being or thing (piyameva sattaṃ vā saṅkhāraṃ vā nissāya uppajjati).
